pos: n. (Hungarian coronation city on the Danube, German Pressburg, Slovak Bratislava; seat of the tribunal that condemned the Protestant ministers in 1674)
etymology: Hungarian Pozsony, from a personal name Poson; German Pressburg, the fortress of Braslav; the site is the castle rock where the Danube leaves the Carpathians.
biblical_def: Pozsony became the capital of Habsburg Hungary after Buda fell to the Turk, the place where the kings were crowned, the Diet met and the royal courts sat. Its Reformation was early and strong among the German burghers, and for a century the city had its Lutheran church, school and preachers under the protection of the Peace of Vienna. In the 1670s the Habsburg government turned on that settlement. Taking the Wesselenyi conspiracy as a warrant, it declared the Protestant churches of Hungary forfeit, and in 1673 and again in 1674 summoned the Lutheran and Reformed ministers and schoolmasters of the kingdom before an extraordinary tribunal at Pozsony. Hundreds were cited. They were charged with treason and offered three ways out: convert to Rome, resign their ministry and leave the country, or be condemned. Most chose exile or imprisonment; a few hundred signed. Those who would do neither were sentenced to the galleys, and the march to Naples began from the prisons of this city. The dictionary enters Pozsony as a case to be remembered precisely: a persecution carried out not by a mob but by a court, with citations, counsel, written charges and a judgment, which is the form religious persecution usually takes in a state with lawyers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tribunal as a court of justice; to cite as to summon to appear in a court; and recantation as the retracting of a declaration or opinion.
webster_full: TRIBUNAL, n. [L. tribunal.] The seat of a judge; a court of justice; the bench on which judges sit.
CITE, v.t. [L. cito.] To call upon officially or authoritatively to appear; to summon; to call to appear in a court.
RECANTATION, n. The act of recanting; a retraction of a declaration, opinion or proposition; a declaration contradicting a former one.
FORFEIT, v.t. [L. foris factum.] To lose or render confiscable by some fault, offense or crime; to lose the right to by misconduct.
GALLEY, n. A low flat-built vessel with one deck, navigated with sails and oars, formerly used in the Mediterranean.

corruption_summary: Hungarian coronation city where an extraordinary Habsburg tribunal cited, tried and sentenced the Protestant ministry of the kingdom in 1673 and 1674.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the use of lawful forms to do an unlawful thing. The Pozsony tribunal did not deny the Protestant ministers a hearing; it gave them one, with a charge sheet, and convicted them of treason for holding their livings. That is worse than a riot, because it enlists the conscience of a whole legal class and leaves a record which the next generation can cite as precedent. The dictionary names the Habsburg policy of the 1670s as persecution and refuses the defence that it was conducted according to law. “They shall put you out of the synagogues” (Joh 16:2) is also a formal act of a lawful court.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the limit of the magistrate. The civil power is ordained of God for the punishment of evildoers, and a man's continuing in the ministry to which his church has called him is not an evil deed. Where the sword is turned upon worship it has left its sphere, and the subject's duty of obedience, which is real, does not extend to resigning the preaching of the gospel at a court's order.

pos: n. (Upper Hungarian free city, Slovak Presov; seat of a Lutheran college, and of the military tribunal of 1687)
etymology: Hungarian Eperjes, from eper, a strawberry, the fruit of the hills about the town; Slovak Presov, of uncertain origin.
biblical_def: Eperjes was one of the five royal free cities of Upper Hungary, a German and Slovak town on the salt road, and it took the Reformation early and almost entirely. Its chief ornament was the collegium founded in 1667 by the Lutheran estates of the region, intended to be the university Protestant Hungary was never allowed to have; it drew teachers of reputation and lasted, in its first form, only until the Jesuits were given the building in 1673. Fourteen years later the town gave its name to a worse thing. After the collapse of the Thokoly rising, the imperial general Antonio Caraffa set up a court at Eperjes in 1687 which, on confessions taken under torture, executed a succession of the town's and the region's leading Protestant citizens in the market place over several months. It was remembered in Hungarian as the Eperjes slaughter, and it did more than any argument to fix the identification of the Habsburg cause with Rome and the Hungarian cause with the gospel. The dictionary keeps Eperjes for the pairing of its two monuments: a college built by a church that wanted its sons taught, and a scaffold built by a state that had decided the church should not exist.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a scaffold as a temporary stage for the execution of a criminal; torture as extreme pain inflicted to extort a confession; and a college as a society of persons engaged in learning.
webster_full: SCAFFOLD, n. A temporary gallery or stage raised for the execution of a criminal; any temporary elevated platform.
TORTURE, n. [L. tortura.] Extreme pain; anguish of body; particularly, severe pain inflicted judicially, to extort a confession.
COLLEGE, n. [L. collegium.] A collection or society of men invested with certain powers; an edifice appropriated to students acquiring learning.
FREE CITY, n. A city having its own magistrates and privileges, and not subject to the jurisdiction of a feudal lord.
WITNESS, n. [Sax. witnes.] Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; one who sees or knows and testifies.

corruption_summary: Upper Hungarian free city whose Lutheran college was taken in 1673 and whose leading Protestants were executed by Caraffa's court in 1687.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The genuine difficulty is the use later made of Eperjes. Hungarian national writing has made the slaughter a purely national grievance, and Habsburg apologists have made it a measure against armed rebellion, which some of the accused had indeed supported. Both readings leave out the deciding fact: the confessions were taken by torture, the charge was not separable from the men's religion, and a court whose evidence is extorted has ceased to be a court. The dictionary names it an execution of Protestants for being Protestants, without pretending that every man killed was a saint.

The principle to recover is the one Christ gave the church for such seasons: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10). It is not a promise of deliverance. It is a promise that the account is kept and the reward is certain, which is the only thing that holds a man in a market place at the end of such a trial. The college and the scaffold in one small town are the Reformation's two normal costs: it has to teach its children, and it has to bury some of them.

pos: n. (Upper Hungarian free city of the Szepes, Slovak Levoca, German Leutschau; a Lutheran town and a centre of Hungarian printing)
etymology: Hungarian Locse, Slovak Levoca, from a Slavic root for the left hand or the left bank; German Leutschau is a borrowing of the same.
biblical_def: Locse was the chief of the towns of the Szepes, the German-settled upland county below the Tatras, and it went over to the Reformation with the rest of them in the 1540s, holding the Lutheran confession in the form set out by the Confessio Pentapolitana of the five free cities. Its parish church of St James kept its medieval altars and its Lutheran preaching together for three centuries, which is an unusual survival and a Lutheran rather than a Reformed instinct. Its greater service was the press. From 1625 the Brewer family printed at Locse for a hundred years, and because the town was far from Vienna and under the protection of the Protestant estates, it could print what Pozsony and Vienna would not license: Hungarian and Slovak hymnbooks, catechisms, Bibles, school texts, funeral sermons and the devotional books by which the Protestant households of Upper Hungary were held together after their ministers were driven out. The dictionary keeps Locse for that. When the pulpits of a province are closed by an edict, what is left in the house is a printed book, and the town that owns the press has become, without intending it, the province's minister.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a press as a printing machine; a hymn as a song of adoration to God; and to license as to permit by grant of authority.
webster_full: PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which paper is impressed by types; hence, the art or business of printing and publishing.
HYMN, n. [Gr. a song of praise.] A song or ode in honor of God, and among pagans, in honor of some deity; a religious song.
LICENSE, v.t. To permit by grant of authority; to remove legal restraint by a grant of permission; to authorize to print.
CATECHISM, n. [Gr. to instruct by word of mouth.] A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
HOUSEHOLD, n. Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family; a family living together.

corruption_summary: Szepes free city whose Brewer press printed for a century the Hungarian and Slovak books the Protestant households of Upper Hungary lived on.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the sentimental one: the printing press treated as the hero of the Reformation, as though a technology had produced a revival. It did not. The press multiplied what men had already resolved to say, and it multiplied error just as efficiently—Locse's own century saw antitrinitarian and enthusiast books printed as cheaply as catechisms. A press is a servant whose master is the doctrine fed into it.

The principle to recover is the household use of the printed word. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16) was fulfilled in Upper Hungary, when the pulpits were shut, by fathers reading a Locse hymnbook and catechism to their families. The dictionary holds that the family's worship is not a substitute for the church's and that it is the thing which keeps a church in being when the church's assemblies are forbidden.

pos: n. (Upper Hungarian free city, Slovak Bardejov, German Bartfeld; where Leonhard Stockel taught and the Confessio Pentapolitana was drawn)
etymology: Hungarian Bartfa, Slovak Bardejov, probably from a Slavic personal name Bardej; German Bartfeld is a folk reading of the same as Bart, a beard, and Feld, a field.
biblical_def: Bartfa was a walled German free city on the Polish road, rich on the Cracow trade, and the first of the five Upper Hungarian cities to receive the Reformation outright. Its schoolmaster from 1539 until his death in 1560 was Leonhard Stockel, a native of the town who had studied at Wittenberg in Melanchthon's house and came home to make the Bartfa school the best in the kingdom; he wrote its ordinances, taught by catechism and by acted Latin plays on biblical subjects, and trained a generation of Upper Hungarian ministers and magistrates. His other service was the Confessio Pentapolitana of about 1549, the confession of the five free cities, drawn chiefly by him and presented to the king as the faith of the towns—a Lutheran confession framed to show the crown that the cities were not Anabaptists and that their religion was the old catholic faith purged, not a novelty. The town also had a press, and after Stockel a long line of rectors. The dictionary enters Bartfa as the clearest instance in Hungary of the Reformation carried by a schoolmaster and a town council together, and of a confession written not to divide but to make a church intelligible to the magistrate who had the power to destroy it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as a formulary comprising the articles of faith; a schoolmaster as the man who presides over a school; and a corporation as a body politic with perpetual succession.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. [L. confessio.] The acknowledgment of a belief; a formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised, and to which assent is given.
SCHOOLMASTER, n. The man who presides over and teaches a school; a teacher; a preceptor; one who disciplines.
CORPORATION, n. A body politic or corporate, formed and authorized by law to act as a single person; a town or city with such privileges.
ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a statute or law made by a town council or other authority.
PURGE, v.t. [L. purgo.] To cleanse; to clear of impurities; to clear from accusation or the imputation of guilt.

Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
corruption_summary: Upper Hungarian free city where Leonhard Stockel taught for twenty-one years and drew the Confessio Pentapolitana of the five cities.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary differs from the Bartfa confession where any Lutheran confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession differ: on baptism, on the manner of Christ's presence in the Supper, and on the authority of the magistrate in the church. Those are real differences and the dictionary does not call them tensions. It also notes what the Pentapolitana got right and what Reformed confessions of the same decades sometimes got wrong: it was written for the magistrate to read, in the plainest form the writers could manage, and it did not mistake obscurity for depth.

The principle to recover is the duty of a church to be intelligible. “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) assumes a faith that can be stated, and a confession is the stating of it. A congregation which cannot say in writing what it believes has nothing to contend for, and will be described instead by its enemies.

pos: n. (Upper Hungarian free city under the High Tatras, Slovak Kezmarok, German Käsmark; a Lutheran town and seat of an articular church)
etymology: German Käsmarkt, the cheese market; Hungarian Kesmark and Slovak Kezmarok are borrowings of the German name of the market under the mountains.
biblical_def: Kesmark lies under the High Tatras, a German market town which received the Reformation in the 1540s and held the Lutheran confession through everything that followed. Its interest for the dictionary is what the Hungarian law did to its worship. By the articles of the Diet of Sopron in 1681, the Habsburg government conceded to the Protestants of each county not freedom of worship but two places in which it might be exercised—the so-called articular places. The churches built in them were restricted by later regulation in a way designed to humiliate: outside the town walls, of wood without iron nails, with no tower and no bell, and the door not facing the street. Kesmark built such a church, a timber barn holding a great congregation, and used it for a century and a half; the restriction produced, as restrictions sometimes do, a remarkable thing, a wooden hall with galleries and a painted roof filled every Sunday by people who had walked in from a whole county. The dictionary enters Kesmark for the lesson of the articular church. A state may grant worship on terms meant as an insult, and a church may take the terms, build the barn, and fill it; and in the end it is the barn that is remembered and the insult that is forgotten.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an article as a clause in a contract or treaty; a bell as a vessel of metal sounded by a stroke; and a sanctuary as a sacred place, a place of worship.
webster_full: ARTICLE, n. [L. articulus.] A single clause in a contract, account, system of regulations, treaty or other writing; a particular.
BELL, n. [Sax. bell.] A vessel or hollow body of cast metal, used for making sounds, and usually hung in a steeple or tower.
SANCTUARY, n. [L. sanctuarium.] A sacred place; a dwelling consecrated to God; a place of worship; a place of protection.
TIMBER, n. That sort of wood which is proper for buildings; wood squared or fit for squaring, for the frame of a building.
HUMILIATE, v.t. [L. humilis.] To humble; to lower in condition; to depress; to make low or abject.

corruption_summary: Tatra free city which built one of the articular wooden churches allowed by the Diet of Sopron in 1681, without tower, bell or iron nail.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the toleration designed as a humiliation. The articular system conceded the substance of worship and then attached conditions calculated to mark the worshippers as a tolerated inferiority: no bell to call them, no tower to be seen, the building pushed outside the wall. It is the same policy by which a state in any century concedes a right and then regulates its exercise into contempt, and it should be recognised under whatever modern form it takes.

The principle to recover is that the church's dignity is not in its fabric. “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) is the answer to the whole apparatus of towers and bells, and a congregation that knows it can accept a wooden barn without accepting the judgment the barn was meant to express. The dictionary adds the other half: the magistrate who imposed the terms was wrong to impose them, and gratitude for the concession is not approval of the insult.

pos: n. (Upper Hungarian county town on the Vag, Slovak Trencin; a Protestant centre of the north-west until the Jesuit settlement of 1655)
etymology: Hungarian Trencsen, Slovak Trencin, from a Slavic root, the name recorded in antiquity as Laugaricio on the castle rock above the Vag.
biblical_def: Trencsen stands under a castle on the Vag in the north-west of old Hungary, on the road from Moravia, and that road made its church history. The Reformation reached it early from the Moravian and Silesian side, the county nobility took it, and for a century the town was one of the centres from which the Lutheran church of the Slovak-speaking counties was supplied with ministers and books. The Synod of Zsolna, which organised that church, was held thirty miles away under the protection of the Thurzo family, whose seat was the county. Trencsen also received the refugees the other way: Bohemian and Moravian exiles after 1620 came down the same road, and the town's printing and preaching were strengthened by men who had lost everything in the Habsburg settlement of their own country. From 1655 the balance turned, a Jesuit college was established in the town, the magistracy was pressed, and over two generations Trencsen became a Catholic county seat with a Protestant minority. The dictionary enters it as a plain case of the Counter-Reformation's actual method in Hungary, which was not usually the scaffold: it was a college, a patron, a lawsuit over a church building, and fifty years of patience.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a refugee as one who flees to a place of safety; a seminary as a place of education; and patience as the suffering of afflictions with a calm mind.
webster_full: REFUGEE, n. [Fr. refugie.] One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who, in times of persecution or political commotion, flees to a foreign country.
SEMINARY, n. [L. seminarium, a seed-plot.] A place of education; any school, academy, college or university in which young persons are instructed.
PATIENCE, n. [L. patientia.] The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.
PATRON, n. One who countenances, supports or protects; a guardian; an advocate; one who has the gift of a church living.
LAWSUIT, n. An action in law for the recovery of a supposed right; a process in law instituted by a party to compel another to do him justice.

corruption_summary: North-western Hungarian county seat, a Protestant centre strengthened by Moravian exiles, which a Jesuit college and fifty years of pressure turned Catholic.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the Counter-Reformation's patient method, which is more instructive than its violent one. In Hungary, outside the crises of the 1670s and 1687, the old religion was recovered chiefly by founding schools the Protestants could not match, converting or replacing the landlord who held the right of presentation, and litigating over the ownership of church buildings until the Protestant congregation was worshipping in a barn. There is no scaffold in that account and it was far more effective than the scaffold. A church that prepares itself only against persecution will be taken apart by a school and a lawyer.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is perseverance in the ordinary. “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9) is the answer to a fifty-year campaign, and the answer is not a counter-campaign but a church that keeps teaching its children, training its ministers and holding its ground through three generations of discouragement.

pos: n. (Upper Hungarian town, Hungarian Zsolna; where the synod of 1610 organised the Lutheran church of the Slovak counties)
etymology: Slovak Zilina, Hungarian Zsolna, from a Slavic root zila, a vein or watercourse, of the rivers meeting there.
biblical_def: Zilina stands where the Rajcanka and the Kysuca meet the Vag, and it is remembered for one assembly. By 1610 the Lutheran congregations of the Slovak-speaking counties of Upper Hungary had been in existence for sixty years without a government of their own: they were legally still parishes of Catholic dioceses whose bishops would not ordain or visit them, so that ordination, discipline and the examination of ministers had no settled authority anywhere. Under the protection of the palatine Gyorgy Thurzo, a synod met at Zsolna in March 1610 and provided one. It divided the ten counties into three districts, elected a superintendent for each with power to ordain and to visit, ordered the examination of candidates and the keeping of records, and required the Augsburg Confession of all. The Catholic primate protested that the assembly had usurped his jurisdiction, and he was right in law; the synod answered that a church which cannot ordain cannot continue, and it was right in substance. The dictionary enters Zilina for that necessity. A congregation may live a long time on inherited order, but there comes a point at which it must either constitute its own government according to Scripture or dissolve, and the hour at which it does so is always an hour of apparent usurpation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as a council of ecclesiastics; jurisdiction as legal power or authority; and to ordain as to invest with ministerial function.
webster_full: SYNOD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion; in Scotland, a court consisting of several presbyteries.
JURISDICTION, n. [L. jurisdictio.] The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing laws; extent of power.
ORDAIN, v.t. [L. ordino.] To appoint; to set apart for an office; to invest with ministerial function or sacerdotal power.
DISTRICT, n. [L. districtus.] A portion of territory marked out or defined by lines; a circuit or territory within which one may compel appearance.
USURP, v.t. [L. usurpo.] To seize and hold in possession by force or without right; to take or assume authority not one's own.
scriptures: Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.
Eph 4:11
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
corruption_summary: Upper Hungarian town where the synod of 1610 gave the Slovak Lutheran congregations superintendents, ordination and discipline of their own.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary differs from the Zsolna settlement on its form. The synod elected superintendents with ordinary jurisdiction over other presbyters; the New Testament uses elder, bishop and overseer of one office, and “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) is a plurality in each place. The 1689 London Baptist Confession knows elders and deacons and no superintendent. What the dictionary affirms with the synod is the prior point: ordination belongs to the church and not to a bishop who refuses to exercise it, and a congregation deprived of order must constitute order.

The principle to recover is that church government is a matter of obedience and not of permission. The primate's protest was legally sound and theologically empty, for he was complaining of a jurisdiction he had declined to use. Where an existing authority will neither ordain a church's ministers nor discipline its members, it has vacated the office; the church that then acts has not usurped anything, and the charge of schism properly lies against the party that abandoned the duty first.

pos: n. pl. (the Hungarian Protestant ministers and schoolmasters condemned in 1674 and sent to the Naples galleys, released in February 1676)
etymology: Galley, from Late Latin galea, an oared warship; the Hungarian name galyarab prediktorok, galley-slave preachers, is the title under which they are remembered.
biblical_def: Of the hundreds of Hungarian Lutheran and Reformed ministers and schoolmasters cited before the Pozsony tribunal in 1673 and 1674, a remnant would neither convert nor resign nor accept exile. Some were held in fortress prisons; about forty were sent south in the spring of 1675, driven on foot across Styria and the Italian states in chains, shown in the towns as condemned criminals, and sold to the Spanish galley fleet at Naples. Several died on the road and several at the oar. Their case became known in Protestant Europe through letters smuggled out and through the Dutch and Swiss churches, and the Dutch Republic took it up as a matter of state. In February 1676 the admiral Michiel de Ruyter, then in the Mediterranean, demanded and obtained the release of the twenty-six survivors, took them aboard, and landed them at Naples a free company; they made their way to Venice, Zurich and the German universities, and a few lived to return to Hungary after the Diet of Sopron. Their narratives were printed and read for two centuries. The dictionary enters them as the clearest instance in the whole period of a refusal that cost everything and conceded nothing: men who were offered their liberty, their livings and their homes for a signature, and who did not sign.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a galley-slave as a person condemned to work at the oar; a confessor as one who makes profession of his faith under persecution; and ransom as the release of a captive by paying a price.
webster_full: GALLEY-SLAVE, n. A person condemned for a crime to work at the oar on board of a galley; hence, one in the lowest condition of servitude.
CONFESSOR, n. One who makes a profession of his faith in the Christian religion; one who avows his religion in the face of danger.
RANSOM, n. [L. redemptio.] The money or price paid for the redemption of a prisoner or slave, or for goods captured by an enemy.
CHAIN, n. [L. catena.] A series of links or rings connected; that which binds; a bond; fetters; hence, bondage, slavery.
DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression or any restraint; rescue from danger or any evil.
scriptures: Such as sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron;
Heb 13:3
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death;
And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
corruption_summary: The Hungarian ministers who refused to convert, resign or go into exile, were sold to the Naples galleys in 1675, and were freed by a Dutch admiral in 1676.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the devotional one: the story told as a tale of heroism with the alternative left out. The alternative is what makes it a confession. These men were not seized at random; each was offered a document and could have gone home. The dictionary states the terms plainly, because a reader who does not know what was on the table cannot see what was refused, and because the same offer is made in every generation in some milder currency.

The principle to recover is the church's duty to prisoners. “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3) was obeyed here by the Dutch and Swiss churches, who did not merely pray but wrote, printed, petitioned and at last used a fleet. Intercession that never becomes action is not what the text asks. The dictionary also records the honour of de Ruyter, a plain Reformed seaman who thought the release of twenty-six Hungarian preachers a proper use of a Dutch squadron.

pos: n. (Georg Lani, 1646–1701, Lutheran rector of Korpona, condemned in 1674, who escaped from the march to the galleys and wrote its history)
etymology: Lani, a Latinised form of Hungarian Lanyi; Georg, from Greek georgos, a tiller of the ground.
biblical_def: Georg Lani was a young Slovak Lutheran schoolmaster, rector at Korpona in the mining counties, when the Pozsony citation reached him. He refused the offered recantation, was condemned, and was among the company driven south in 1675 toward the Neapolitan galleys. On the road through the Italian states he escaped from the convoy, was recaptured, imprisoned again, escaped a second time, and made his way across Italy and over the Alps to Germany; he afterwards served Hungarian and Slovak exile congregations and died at Leipzig in 1701. His service to the church was his pen. He wrote and published a detailed narrative of the citation, the trial, the march and the galleys—names, dates, stages of the road, the conduct of the guards, the deaths—and it is from Lani and two or three others that the whole episode is known in detail rather than in rumour. The dictionary enters him for that work. The persecutions of the seventeenth century are known to us exactly where somebody who was in them sat down afterwards and wrote it out; where nobody did, we have an anecdote. A church that does not keep its own records leaves the writing of its history to the party that persecuted it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a narrative as a relation of facts in order; a fugitive as one who flees from danger; and a register as a written account preserved as evidence.
webster_full: NARRATIVE, n. The recital of a story, or a continued account of the particulars of an event or transaction, in the order of time.
FUGITIVE, n. One who flies from his station or duty; one who flees from danger, from persecution, or from pursuit.
REGISTER, n. [L. regestum.] A written account or entry of acts, judgments or proceedings, preserved as authentic evidence.
ESCAPE, v.i. [L. ex and cappa.] To flee from and avoid; to get out of the way; to be free from danger or confinement.
TESTIMONY, n. [L. testimonium.] A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
scriptures: Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Jer 36:4
Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah: and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD, which he had spoken unto him, upon a roll of a book.
Many are the afflictions of the righteous: but the LORD delivereth him out of them all.
corruption_summary: Slovak Lutheran rector who refused the recantation, escaped twice from the march to the galleys, and wrote the detailed history of the whole proceeding.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest question about Lani is his flight, and the dictionary answers it plainly rather than piously. Escaping from a convoy is not a failure of confession; he had already refused the recantation, which was the point at which the faith was at stake, and no text requires a man to assist his captors. The confessors who stayed at the oar and the confessor who got over the Alps and published the record were both serving the same church, and the second did a work the first could not do.

The principle to recover is the duty of written testimony. “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2) is a command, and the church has usually obeyed it late. Lani wrote names, dates and stages, which is why his account could not be waved away. The dictionary holds that an afflicted congregation should keep its minutes, its letters and its registers as carefully as its collections, because in fifty years they will be the only answer to an official history.

pos: n. (Stephan Pilarik, 1615–1693, Slovak Lutheran pastor, carried off by Tatars in 1663 and exiled in 1673, author of a narrative of his deliverances)
etymology: Pilarik, a Slovak surname from pilar, a sawyer; Stephan, from Greek stephanos, a crown.
biblical_def: Stephan Pilarik was a Slovak Lutheran minister of the Hungarian lowland and the Danube counties, pastor at Senica and afterwards at Bekescsaba and Szenice, in the generation that met both of Hungary's afflictions. In 1663, when the Turkish army and its Tatar auxiliaries overran the country, he was taken captive with a column of prisoners and driven away, was separated and sold, and came back alive by a series of escapes and ransoms which he afterwards wrote out as the work of providence rather than of his own wit. Ten years later the Habsburg proceedings of 1673 reached him, and he was driven out of Hungary altogether; he spent his last twenty years as a pastor to German congregations in Saxony and Silesia and died at Neusalz in 1693. His narrative, published in German, is the book by which he is remembered: an account of his own captivity, losses and preservations, written to be read in households, in which every deliverance is referred to God and no revenge is asked against either the Turk or the emperor. The dictionary enters him because his life forced the question which the Hungarian church had to answer twice in one lifetime: what a believer owes to God when the affliction comes first from the infidel and then from the Christian prince.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines captivity as the state of being a prisoner; providence as the care of God over his creatures; and deliverance as release from captivity or any evil.
webster_full: CAPTIVITY, n. [L. captivitas.] The state of being a prisoner or of being in the power of an enemy by force or the fate of war; subjection; bondage.
PROVIDENCE, n. [L. providentia.] The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; a watching over and ordering of events.
DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression or any restraint; rescue from danger; the act of freeing.
RANSOM, v.t. To redeem from captivity or punishment by paying a price; to buy out of servitude.
EXILE, n. [L. exilium.] Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country; the person banished.
scriptures: Such as sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron;
Rom 8:28
And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
Lam 3:22
It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
corruption_summary: Slovak Lutheran pastor carried off by Tatars in 1663 and expelled by the Habsburg proceedings in 1673, who wrote his deliverances as providence.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live temptation in such a life is the one Pilarik resisted: to let the second affliction decide the doctrine. A man robbed by the Turk and then exiled by the emperor has every provocation to make his theology a grievance, and much Hungarian Protestant writing after 1673 does exactly that. Pilarik referred both calamities to the hand of God and asked what they were for, which is the prophets' question and not the politician's.

The principle to recover is the reading of one's own life by providence. “And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God” (Rom 8:28) is not a sentiment to be embroidered; it is a rule of interpretation applied to captivity, loss of goods and banishment. The dictionary commends the form Pilarik chose—a household narrative, written for his children, in which God is the agent and the author is the subject acted upon.
